CausalChain: CTNNB1 exon 3 mutation in HepG2 cells -> Dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin signaling -> Altered transcription of drug-metabolizing genes (e.g., CYP enzymes) -> Reduced phase I metabolic activity -> Impaired xenobiotic clearance and chemoresistance -> Hepatoblastoma-like phenotype
Hypothesis: The CTNNB1 exon 3 mutation-driven dysregulation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway in HepG2 cells underlies their deficient cytochrome P450 activity, thereby contributing to a hepatoblastoma phenotype with intrinsic chemoresistance; modulation of this pathway may restore metabolic function and improve therapeutic responses.
Abstract: HepG2 cells, originally established as models of liver cancer, exhibit genetic and metabolic features that align more closely with hepatoblastoma than with hepatocellular carcinoma. Notably, a recurrent CTNNB1 exon 3 mutation in HepG2 cells results in dysregulation of the Wnt/β‐catenin signaling pathway. This dysregulation appears to impair the expression of key drug‐metabolizing enzymes such as cytochrome P450 isoforms, leading to altered xenobiotic processing and potential chemoresistance. We propose that targeted modulation of the Wnt pathway in HepG2 cells may restore metabolic enzyme expression, thereby enhancing drug sensitivity and providing a more predictive model for hepatoblastoma. Such insights into the interplay between oncogenic signaling and metabolic competency could pave the way for novel therapeutic interventions in pediatric liver cancers.
